find: — examiners deduct marks for descriptions that simply state what happens without explaining why it matters.
replace: — an Explain answer must contain reasoning, so a point stated without a reason will not gain the mark.
note: F1: Edexcel marks positively; nothing is deducted. Spec Appendix 1 defines Explain as needing justification with linked marking points.

find: Your specification identifies four key benefits of structuring programs using subprograms.
replace: Your specification says you must understand the benefits of using subprograms. Four benefits come up again and again.
note: F2: spec 1.1.2 lists no benefits at all, so the four cannot be presented as a spec list.

expect: Name the four benefits of using subprograms listed in the specification.
value: Name four benefits of using subprograms.
note: F3: same as F2 - the specification lists none.
F4: Identify carries 1 mark for each item; the stem asks for two sub-problems, so the tariff is 2 marks.

expect:
Mastering: Any two valid sub-problems, each clearly identifiable and distinct, e.g. searching for a book, recording a loan, sending overdue reminders, managing member accounts, reserving books. 1 mark for each valid sub-problem (up to 2 marks for this question in exam context, but listed as 1-mark Identify type — accept any one clearly valid sub-problem for 1 mark).
Secure: One valid sub-problem.
Developing: Vague — e.g. 'looking up books'.
Emerging: Describes a feature rather than a sub-problem.
value:
Mastering: Any two valid sub-problems, each clearly identifiable and distinct, e.g. searching for a book, recording a loan, sending overdue reminders, managing member accounts, reserving books. 1 mark for each valid sub-problem, up to 2 marks.
Secure: One valid sub-problem.
Developing: Vague — e.g. 'looking up books'.

note: F4: removes the mark scheme arguing with its own tariff label.

find: In a flowchart showing a loop, an arrow curves back upward from the “No” exit of the diamond to an earlier process step.
replace: In a flowchart showing a loop, an arrow curves back to an earlier step from the exit that keeps the loop going. In a “while” loop the diamond tests the condition for carrying on, so the “Yes” exit loops back and the “No” exit leaves the loop.
note: F5: the loop-back arrow does not always leave the No exit; as written the rule makes a student draw the standard while loop the wrong way round.

find: data-revision-tip="Cover this and write out all six arithmetic operators and four relational operators from memory, giving an example value for each."
replace: data-revision-tip="Cover this and write out all seven arithmetic operators and six relational operators from memory, giving an example value for each."
note: F6: spec 1.2.3 names seven arithmetic and six relational operators, and the key fact beside the tip already lists seven and six.

find: Examiners award marks for correct logic, not correct syntax.
replace: In a pseudocode answer it is the logic that earns the marks, not exact syntax. Questions that ask you to write or amend program code are different — there you write Python 3, the language of the Programming Language Subset.
note: F7: true for pseudocode only. Paper 1 also sets Write and Amend code items where the PLS notation matters.
F8: the stem asks the student to write an algorithm. Write carries 1 to 6 marks, so 4 marks stands.
F9: 'Complete an Algorithm' is not an Edexcel command word and nothing is supplied to complete; the stem is a Write task.

find: Understanding exactly what each type means is important — examiners report that many students give vague definitions that could apply to more than one type.
replace: Understanding exactly what each type means is important. A definition that could apply to more than one type will not gain the mark.
note: F12: no examiner report is cited and none can be verified; the teaching point survives without the attribution.

find: — a statement of fact alone earns only half the marks.
replace: — a statement of fact on its own does not meet the demand of an Explain question.
note: F13: invented mark-scheme arithmetic; Edexcel publishes no half-marks rule.

expect: A sorted list of student names is: [Ahmed, Clarke, Frost, Green, Khan, Martin, Patel, Singh, Taylor, Wood]. Show the steps a binary search would take to find 'Patel'. State the middle item checked at each step.
value: A sorted list of student names is: [Ahmed, Clarke, Frost, Green, Khan, Martin, Patel, Singh, Taylor, Wood]. Describe the steps a binary search would take to find 'Patel', stating the middle item checked at each step.
note: F14: 'Show' is not an Edexcel command word; Describe is the right verb for giving an account of the steps.
F14: no trace table is supplied or asked for. Describe carries 2 to 4 marks, so 4 marks stands.
F16: Convert means changing one symbolic representation into another; filling in a supplied table is Complete (2 to 6 marks).
F17: it is a truth table, not a trace table; the two are different artefacts.
F18: no algorithm is involved; Complete carries 2 to 6 marks, so 6 marks stands.

note: F19: invented mark-scheme claim; the method advice stands on its own.
